nameStory: Feverfew earned its name from the old English 'feverfugia,' meaning 'fever reducer,' because people traditionally used it to treat fevers and headaches. The scientific name 'parthenium' comes from the Greek word for 'virgin,' possibly referring to its pure white flowers or its supposed medicinal properties for women.
description: Feverfew is a bushy perennial herb that looks like a cheerful miniature daisy garden. It grows 1-3 feet tall with deeply divided, feathery leaves that have a strong, bitter scent when crushed. The plant produces clusters of small white flowers with bright yellow centers, blooming from summer into fall. Originally from the Balkans, it's now commonly grown in gardens and sometimes escapes to grow wild.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white daisy-like flowers about half an inch across with bright yellow button centers, arranged in flat-topped clusters at stem tips

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, feathery leaves that look almost fern-like, with a strong bitter scent and slightly fuzzy texture when crushed between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Bushy, upright plant 1-3 feet tall with multiple branching stems creating a rounded, dense appearance

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny, ribbed seeds without fluffy attachments that scatter from dried flower heads in late summer and fall

habitat: Look for feverfew in gardens, around old homesteads, and along roadsides where it has escaped cultivation. It thrives in well-drained soils and sunny to partially shaded areas, often growing near other garden herbs and wildflowers. In New England, it's most common around settled areas rather than deep in wild forests.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as rosettes of deeply divided leaves with that characteristic bitter scent when crushed.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with abundant clusters of white daisy flowers and full leafy growth.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming into early fall, then sets seed and begins to die back as flowers turn brown and papery.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving dried stems and scattered seeds that will sprout next spring.

funFact: Feverfew flowers are so packed with natural insect-repelling compounds that gardeners often plant it as a living pest control system - it can help keep ants, moths, and even mice away from other plants!
confusionNotes: Feverfew is often confused with chamomile, but feverfew's leaves are much more deeply divided and feathery, while chamomile has thread-like, almost hair-thin leaf segments. Remember: feverfew has 'feathery' leaves (both start with 'fe').
contextualKnowledge: You might see feverfew sold under old names like Chrysanthemum parthenium or Pyrethrum parthenium in garden catalogs, as botanists have moved it between different plant groups over the years. Despite centuries of traditional use for headaches and fevers, modern science hasn't found evidence that it actually works medicinally.
compareHints: Unlike its cousin tansy which has button-like yellow flowers with no white petals, feverfew always has the classic white daisy appearance. Tansy also grows much taller (up to 5 feet) and has a more aggressive spreading habit, while feverfew stays more compact and well-behaved in gardens.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Tansy differs from its cousin feverfew by having purely yellow button flowers instead of feverfew's white daisy-like blooms with yellow centers.
Compared to common tansy, dune tansy is much shorter and more compact, adapted for harsh coastal conditions rather than inland meadows.
